1.pericope_label: I waited patiently for the Lord; and he inclined unto me, and heard my cry... Many, O Lord my God, are thy wonderful works which thou hast done

schools.summary: Ellicott identifies the doubled verb as the infinitive absolute — 'I waited and waited' — and argues the whole scene into metaphor, since the rock is 'the common image of security, the occurrence of which makes it probable that the pit and clay are also not realities'. Delitzsch takes David as author 'though not without some hesitation', placing him between rescue and continuing peril.

Calvin rejects the reading that makes the danger a sickness and takes it for 'a multitude of dangers', drawing from the repeated verb the doctrine that God may 'of design keep us in suspense and perplexity' without our losing courage. Gill hears Christ throughout, the patience exercised in the garden and on the cross.

Clarke dates the psalm with the two before it as a thanksgiving for recovery from bodily disease, takes the pit literally as 'the sounding pit', and alone observes that the closing section 'appears to have belonged to another Psalm'. Wesley marks the fifth verse as 'a wall of partition' between David speaking for himself and speaking for the Messiah.

Henry finds neither sickness nor enemies mentioned here and concludes the trouble was inward, 'despondency of spirit under the sense of God's withdrawings'. Spurgeon ranks the patience: 'Job on the dunghill does not equal Jesus on the cross.'

Augustine argues from the standing of the promiser — God is 'a sponsible Promiser; a faithful Paymaster' — and tells the weak to claim mercy as lambs do, 'striking their dams' teats with their heads'.

debates.question: What danger did the psalmist escape?

positions.view: A bodily disease — the same occasion as the two preceding psalms, this being the thanksgiving for the recovery sought there.
Not sickness. 'Some are of opinion, but without good reason, that it ought to be understood of sickness.' Rather a multitude of dangers, even of death.
Inward trouble, since neither sickness nor enemies are named: despondency under God's withdrawings is itself 'a horrible pit and miry clay'.

debates.question: Are the pit and the clay real or figurative?

positions.view: Real enough to describe: 'the sounding pit; where nothing was heard except the howlings of wild beasts, or the hollow sounds of winds.'
Emblems. The rock beside them is a standing figure of security, which makes it probable that pit and clay are 'not realities, but emblems of confusion and danger'.

outliers.view: The only voice to argue the case as a matter of credit — God as a solvent debtor and the believer as 'a dutiful exactor of what is promised'.

themes: I waited patiently for the Lord; and he inclined unto me, and heard my cry.
He brought me up also out of an horrible pit, out of the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock, and established my goings.
And he hath put a new song in my mouth, even praise unto our God: many shall see it, and fear, and shall trust in the Lord.
Blessed is that man that maketh the Lord his trust, and respecteth not the proud, nor such as turn aside to lies.

Many, O Lord my God, are thy wonderful works which thou hast done, and thy thoughts which are to us-ward: they cannot be reckoned up in order unto thee: if I would declare and speak of them, they are more than can be numbered.

6.pericope_label: Sacrifice and offering thou didst not desire; mine ears hast thou opened... I delight to do thy will, O my God: yea, thy law is within my heart

schools.summary: Ellicott rules out both rival readings by one observation: the noun is plural, which 'sets aside the idea of a revelation' and equally 'excludes allusion to the symbolic act by which a slave was devoted to perpetual servitude, because then also only one ear was bored'. He also declares the received rendering of the seventh verse, followed by the Epistle to the Hebrews, one that 'must be abandoned'. Delitzsch reads the passage as a structured negative answer to the question how thanks are to be rendered.
Gill guards the denial, since the sacrifices were once acceptable and the refusal belongs to the time the passage refers to rather than to the institution as such.

Clarke states the Hebrew-Greek divergence without softening it, prefers 'My ears hast thou bored', and reports approvingly a conjecture that the Hebrew is corrupt where the Greek read 'Then, a Body'; he draws the consequence that 'the introduction of the Messiah into the world is the abolition of the law'. Wesley keeps the bored ear and notes the Septuagint's substitution plainly.

Henry sets out what the sacrifices could not do — neither pacify the conscience nor sanctify the nature — their value resting on their reference to Christ. Spurgeon holds both senses of the dug ear at once, and images the obsolescence: the offerings ceased to be of value 'as candles are of no estimation when the sun has arisen'.

debates.question: How can the Hebrew's opened ears become the Greek's prepared body?

positions.view: By textual corruption. The word for ears stands where the original read 'Then, a Body', the two being easy to confuse letter by letter.
It cannot. The Hebrew means 'Ears hast thou dug for me', i.e. the gift of hearing; the plural rules out both the revelation and the pierced-slave readings.
The Hebrew means the bored ear of the slave who refuses his freedom — perpetual service — and the Septuagint's rendering is simply reported as the apostle's.

debates.question: What is 'in the volume of the book'?

positions.view: The Pentateuch, 'for, in David's time no other part of Divine revelation had been committed to writing' — and it speaks throughout of Christ.
Not a prophecy about the speaker at all. 'Lo! I come, bringing the book written for me' — the Law produced as warrant for conduct performed.

outliers.view: The only voice to settle the crux by counting: the plural 'ears' excludes at a stroke both the revelation reading and the pierced-slave reading that the rest of the catena depends on.

themes: Sacrifice and offering thou didst not desire; mine ears hast thou opened: burnt offering and sin offering hast thou not required.
Then said I, Lo, I come: in the volume of the book it is written of me,
I delight to do thy will, O my God: yea, thy law is within my heart.

9.pericope_label: I have preached righteousness in the great congregation... mine iniquities have taken hold upon me, so that I am not able to look up

schools.summary: Ellicott gives the verb its literal sense, 'I have made countenances glad', and notices the form of the passage, clauses following 'like successive wave-beats of praise'. Delitzsch supplies the etymology behind that rendering and observes that here 'petition developes itself out of thanksgiving', the two withholdings answering one another.
Gill keeps the speaker Christ throughout, making the righteousness preached the one 'which Christ himself wrought out', and the innumerable evils the punishment borne as surety for his people.

Clarke takes the great congregation for the Gentiles, the righteousness for justification by faith 'without the deeds of the law', weighs the petition's words one by one, and rejects the placement of the confession of iniquity as belonging to another psalm. Wesley reads the return to David's own case.

Henry marks the change of person and turns the petition into an argument from the greater to the less — 'thou hast not spared thy Son... withhold not thou thy tender mercies then' — and sees the sins arresting the sinner 'as the bailiff does the poor debtor'. Spurgeon keeps Christ speaking, the angel in the garden being the answer to this prayer.

positions.view: The Gentiles, 'contradistinguished from the Jews' — the gospel preached throughout the empire.
The festival assemblies at Jerusalem, when all the males were obliged to appear.
Both: 'not only to the Jews, but also to all nations.'
Christ's, by imputation — the evils being 'the evils of punishment inflicted on him, as the surety and Saviour of his people'.
David's own, arresting him as an officer arrests a debtor.
Neither, here. The words 'could not be said by any person who was exulting in the pardoning mercy of God' — the section belongs elsewhere.

outliers.view: The only voice to reject the passage's placement on psychological grounds, arguing that a man exulting in pardon could not have written these words at this point.

themes: I have preached righteousness in the great congregation: lo, I have not refrained my lips, O Lord, thou knowest.
I have not hid thy righteousness within my heart; I have declared thy faithfulness and thy salvation: I have not concealed thy lovingkindness and thy truth from the great congregation.
Withhold not thou thy tender mercies from me, O Lord: let thy lovingkindness and thy truth continually preserve me.
For innumerable evils have compassed me about: mine iniquities have taken hold upon me, so that I am not able to look up; they are more than the hairs of mine head: therefore my heart faileth me.

13.pericope_label: Be pleased, O Lord, to deliver me: O Lord, make haste to help me... But I am poor and needy; yet the Lord thinketh upon me

schools.summary: Ellicott records as a fact of the text that the passage recurs elsewhere in the Psalter as a separate composition. Delitzsch reads it instead as the natural issue of what precedes — suffering that 'the longer they last, discover him all the more to himself as a sinner' — and describes the wish against the enemies as a recoil, their purpose rebounding 'against the protection of God'.
Gill reads every clause as fulfilled history: the deliverance granted at the resurrection, the shame reserved for the last day, the desolation executed on Jerusalem in fact.

Clarke works word by word — the two adjectives are not synonyms, the divine name is a claim ('my prop, my support'), the verb of thinking is 'meditateth' — and draws the whole argument from it: 'seeing that my miserable state occupies thy heart, it will soon employ thy hand.' Wesley reduces the enemies' shame to their own 'sinful and shameful actions'.

debates.question: Does this section belong to the psalm?

positions.view: Doubtfully. The same passage stands elsewhere in the Psalter as a psalm in its own right, 'with some trifling variations'.
Yes. The petition grows out of the confession before it, and the imprecations continue the same speaker's case.

debates.question: Is the imprecation prayer or prophecy?

positions.view: Prophecy fulfilled: the desolation prayed for fell on Jerusalem, and the shame awaits the last day.
Prayer, and defensive rather than vindictive — that the foes' own purpose 'may as it were rebound against the protection of God and miserably miscarry'.

outliers.view: The only voice to build a whole argument out of the verb 'thinketh', reading it as meditation and inferring from it that the hand must follow the heart.

themes: Be pleased, O Lord, to deliver me: O Lord, make haste to help me.
Let them be ashamed and confounded together that seek after my soul to destroy it; let them be driven backward and put to shame that wish me evil.
Let them be desolate for a reward of their shame that say unto me, Aha, aha.
Let all those that seek thee rejoice and be glad in thee: let such as love thy salvation say continually, The Lord be magnified.
But I am poor and needy; yet the Lord thinketh upon me: thou art my help and my deliverer; make no tarrying, O my God.
